subtype: Approach: uses a checklist for a repeated multi-step process [Action]
passage:
Madhuri: Ishita, people say lab work is all brilliant ideas. What is it really like?

Ishita: A lot of it is a laminated card. Before every experiment I follow the same eleven lines: clean the bench, check the balance reads zero, label the tubes, then buffers, then samples, in that order. Last week I had been up till two with a deadline and my head was cotton. I ran the card anyway. Halfway down I caught myself skipping "label the tubes" because I was in a hurry. The card was right there, so I went back, labelled everything, and the run worked. From memory I would have mixed up two samples.

Madhuri: Does it get boring?

Ishita: Sometimes. But tired me and hurried me do not trust my memory, so I trust the card.

qa.q: How many lines does the card have?
qa.a: Ishita follows the same eleven lines before every experiment.

qa.q: How was Ishita feeling when the head was like cotton, and why use the card anyway?
qa.a: Ishita was very tired and in a hurry, and did not trust memory in that state, so the card was the safer guide.

qa.q: What could a new lab assistant do to keep such a card useful?
qa.a: They could tick each line as it is done and tell the supervisor if a step seems missing or out of date, so the card can be improved.

qa.q: How might someone relying on Ishita's results see this habit?
qa.a: They might feel reassured that the samples are labelled and not mixed up, since Ishita follows every step even when tired.

grounding: Shows a lab assistant following a written checklist for a repeated set-up so no step is skipped when tired or hurried.

subtype: Approach: uses a checklist for a repeated multi-step process [Action]
passage:
I'm Seema, and I work with Uma in the biochemistry teaching lab. She's the lab assistant for the second-year practicals, and I've watched her do the same setup forty times now.
There's a laminated card taped by the fume hood. Twelve steps, in order: gloves, check the balance is zeroed, label the tubes, prepare buffer, warm the water bath, and so on.
Uma knows these steps by heart. But every single time, she runs her finger down the card and says each step softly under her breath. Even at eight in the morning, when she's clearly exhausted.
Last Thursday, the students were already walking in and she was rushing. Her finger stopped at step six. "Water bath," she said. It was still off. She switched it on and waited ten minutes.
The experiment would have failed without it. I don't think she even looked stressed. She just followed the card.

qa.q: How many steps are on the laminated card?
What does Uma saying each step softly suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels calm and careful, trusting the card even when she is tired or rushed, though Seema can only guess.

qa.q: What else could Uma add to the card, and why?
qa.a: She could add a line for the time each step needs, like the water bath's ten minutes, so rushing mornings are planned better.

qa.q: How are the second-year students affected by Uma's card?
qa.a: Their experiment works on Thursday because the water bath was caught in time, even though they never knew it was nearly missed.

grounding: It shows a lab assistant following a checklist to set up an experiment, so steps in the right order are not skipped even when tired or hurried.

subtype: Approach: uses a checklist for a repeated multi-step process [Action]
passage:
Monday. Sharmila started her first week as lab assistant in the college microbiology lab. Thomas, the senior technician, handed her a clipboard. "Checklist for the plating practical. Follow it every time, even when you know it."
She read it: switch on the incubator, wipe the bench, light the burner, sterilise the loop, and on down to twelve steps. She thought it was a bit much.
Wednesday. Forty students arrived early and Sharmila was still setting up. In her hurry she almost poured the plates before sterilising the loop. Her eyes caught line six on the clipboard. She stopped, did it, and only then went on.
Friday. At the end of the week, Thomas asked how the clipboard was working.
"On Wednesday it saved me," she admitted. "I thought I didn't need it. I'm keeping it."

qa.q: What did Thomas hand Sharmila on Monday?
How did Sharmila feel about the checklist at first?
qa.a: She felt it was a bit much and was a little doubtful, thinking she didn't need it.

qa.q: What else could Sharmila do to use the checklist well on busy days?
qa.a: She could start setting up earlier on practical days, so she has time to follow each line calmly.

qa.q: How might Thomas see Sharmila's answer on Friday?
qa.a: Thomas may feel pleased and reassured that the new assistant now trusts the checklist.

grounding: It shows a new lab assistant using a checklist for a repeated setup so steps are not skipped even when rushed.
